titulo: Quiz — Money manners and the con
subtitulo: Las Ramblas, a sprig of rosemary, two beers and a charge that was never on the menu
introPt: Quiz time. A traveller walks down Las Ramblas, gets handed a sprig of rosemary he never asked for, sits down on a terrace for two beers, and then finds a line on the bill that was never on the menu. He deals with all three without raising his voice once — which is exactly the trick. Listen as many times as you like, then answer.
cenario: Barcelona, late afternoon. A woman offers a 'gift' on Las Ramblas; then a terrace, two cañas, and a bill with a cover charge nobody mentioned.

dialogo.es: Toma, un romero. Es un regalo.
dialogo.pinyin: TOH-mah, oon rroh-MEH-roh. ehs oon rreh-GAH-loh
dialogo.pt: — Here, some rosemary. It's a gift. (a woman steps into his path on Las Ramblas)
— No thanks. I'm not interested. (hands in his pockets, still walking)

dialogo.pinyin: BWEH-nahs TAR-dhehs. keh bahn ah toh-MAR
dialogo.pt: — Good afternoon. What are you having? (the waitress, on the terrace)
— The bill, please. (it never comes on its own)

dialogo.pinyin: pehr-DOH-neh, meh TRAH-eh lah KWEHN-tah deh-tah-YAH-dhah
dialogo.pt: — Excuse me, could you bring me the itemised bill?

dialogo.es: Aquí hay un cargo que no estaba en la carta. ¿Qué es?
dialogo.pinyin: ah-KEE ai oon KAR-goh keh noh ehs-TAH-bah en lah KAR-tah. keh ehs?
dialogo.pt: — There's a charge here that wasn't on the menu. What is it?

dialogo.es: Es el cubierto, señor. Dos con cincuenta.
dialogo.pinyin: ehs el koo-BYEHR-toh, seh-NYOR. dohs kon theen-KWEHN-tah
dialogo.pt: — It's the cover charge, sir. Two fifty.

dialogo.es: No estaba anunciado. La hoja de reclamaciones, por favor.
dialogo.pinyin: noh ehs-TAH-bah ah-noon-THYAH-dhoh. lah OH-khah deh rreh-klah-mah-THYOH-nehs, por fah-BOR
dialogo.pt: — It wasn't advertised anywhere. The official complaint form, please. (still seated, still normal volume)

dialogo.es: Perdone usted. Se lo quito. Son catorce euros.
dialogo.pinyin: pehr-DOH-neh oos-TEHDH. seh loh KEE-toh. sohn kah-TOR-theh eh-OO-rohs
dialogo.pt: — I do apologise. I'll take it off. That's fourteen euros.
— Thank you. That's fine as it is. (he hands over fifteen — the round-up, and the whole tipping system)

perguntas.pergunta: A woman steps in front of him on Las Ramblas and presses a sprig of rosemary into his hand, calling it a gift. What does he say — and what do his feet do?
perguntas.es: A woman steps in front of him on Las Ramblas and presses a sprig of rosemary into his hand, calling it a gift. What does he say — and what do his feet do?
opcoes: 'No, gracias. No me interesa.' — and he keeps walking
'Gracias' — and he takes it, to be polite
He stops and politely explains that he doesn't want it
He hands over a couple of euros to make it go away
perguntas.explica: This is 'el romero', and it runs on your manners, not on force. Take it, stop, or argue and you are inside the transaction — often with a second person working your bag while the first holds your hand. Hands in your pockets, don't extend your hand, don't slow down. If it's already in your hand: drop it or give it back, and keep going.

perguntas.pergunta: The waitress says 'Son dieciséis con cincuenta.' How much is the bill?
perguntas.es: The waitress says 'Son dieciséis con cincuenta.' How much is the bill?
perguntas.explica: 'cincuenta' is 50, and in Spain it carries the 'th' of 'think': theen-KWEHN-tah. 'sesenta' (60) does not. You never have to produce that sound — but you do have to hear it, because 5, 12 to 15, 50, 100 and 'céntimos' all carry it, and those are the numbers on every bar bill in the country.

perguntas.pergunta: A number on the bill looks wrong. What does he ask for FIRST?
perguntas.es: A number on the bill looks wrong. What does he ask for FIRST?
opcoes: The itemised bill — 'la cuenta detallada'
The official complaint form
The manager
The local police
perguntas.explica: Rung one of the ladder, and it is deliberately gentle: it accuses nobody and hands everyone an elegant way out. About half the time the problem quietly evaporates on the walk to the till. The whole trick of the ladder is that your voice does not change between the rungs.

perguntas.pergunta: What is 'el cubierto' — and why does he object to it?
perguntas.es: What is 'el cubierto' — and why does he object to it?
opcoes: A cover charge, legal only if you were told before you sat down
A tip that Spanish law adds automatically
VAT, which is always added at the end in Spain
The terrace surcharge, which can never be charged
perguntas.explica: 'Servicio' and 'cubierto' are only chargeable where the regional rules allow it AND you were informed in advance — printed on the menu or on the price list at the door. It wasn't. Note the contrast: a terrace surcharge IS perfectly legal, provided it is posted. Which is why you read the price list before you sit down.

perguntas.pergunta: 'La hoja de reclamaciones, por favor.' Why does that sentence end the argument?
perguntas.es: 'La hoja de reclamaciones, por favor.' Why does that sentence end the argument?
opcoes: It's an official three-copy form, and one copy goes to the regional authority that inspects and licenses the business
It automatically fines the business several thousand euros
It legally obliges the restaurant to refund the entire bill
It summons the local police to your table
perguntas.explica: It works before you have written a single word on it: you are not complaining, you are opening a file with the body that licenses them — so for a lot of businesses, fixing it at the table is simply cheaper. Refusing to hand one over is an offence in its own right, separate from whether you were right about the bill. Say it sitting down, at normal volume, without the apologetic smile.

perguntas.pergunta: According to UK Foreign Office advice, a genuine Spanish police officer will ask to see…
perguntas.es: According to UK Foreign Office advice, a genuine Spanish police officer will ask to see…
opcoes: Your ID — never your wallet or purse
Your wallet, to check for counterfeit notes
Your bank card and your PIN
Your hotel key card
perguntas.explica: Thieves posing as officers ask for the wallet — usually in English, usually in pairs, with a badge flashed and withdrawn fast. You don't hand it over and you don't get physical. You say: 'Enséñeme su placa. Vamos a la comisaría.' A real officer is perfectly happy to walk to the station; a fake one evaporates.

perguntas.pergunta: The bill lands at fourteen euros, he hands over fifteen and says 'Está bien así.' Is that the right amount to leave?
perguntas.es: The bill lands at fourteen euros, he hands over fifteen and says 'Está bien así.' Is that the right amount to leave?
opcoes: Yes — rounding up is the entire system in Spain
No, he should have left 20%
No, he should have left 15%
No — leaving anything at all is odd in Spain
perguntas.explica: Round up, or leave nothing at all. Both are completely normal, because Spanish hospitality staff are on a salary and a collective agreement — the tip is a bonus, not the wage. Twenty per cent doesn't read as generous; it reads as an accent. Bonus: 'Está bien así' commits you to neither tú nor usted, which is why it works everywhere.
